name: Guangzhou
info: Guangzhou, also called Canton, is the capital of Guangdong in southern China, on the Pearl River. Founded as Panyu in 214 BCE, it was a capital of Nanyue, a major port and the only legal site of foreign trade from 1757 to 1842.

facts.founded: Founded as Panyu on the eastern bank of the Pearl River in 214 BCE. A settlement now known as Nanwucheng was present in the area by 1100 BCE.
facts.where: On the Pearl River in the delta of south-central Guangdong, southern China, about 120 kilometres north-west of Hong Kong and 145 kilometres north of Macau.
facts.known: Panyu, capital of Nanyue; a port of the Silk Road; the sack of 878; the Southern Han; the Canton System and the Thirteen Factories; the First Opium War; the revolutionary base of Sun Yat-sen and the Kuomintang
facts.today: Guangzhou is the capital and largest city of Guangdong and a city of subprovincial status.

t: The town of Panyu was founded in 214 BCE as the seat of a Qin commandery, became the capital of the kingdom of Nanyue under Zhao Tuo in 204 BCE and was annexed by the Han in 111 BCE.
From the Tang dynasty it was a port tied to the Middle East and Southeast Asia, and from 1757 to 1842 the Thirteen Factories there were the only legal place to conduct foreign trade with China.
After the First Opium War it lost its monopoly to Hong Kong and Shanghai, but it remained an entrepôt and became a base of Sun Yat-sen and the Kuomintang in the 1920s.
dyk: The city's nicknames, the City of Rams and the City of the Immortals, come from a story of five immortals who rode five rams and introduced rice cultivation to the area, around the time of the city's foundation.
ev: Panyu is founded on the eastern bank of the Pearl River as the seat of the Qin Empire's Nanhai Commandery
General Zhao Tuo establishes the kingdom of Nanyue and makes Panyu its capital
Han armies take Panyu and annex Nanyue
Arab and Persian pirates sack the city
The rebel Huang Chao takes the city and about 200,000 foreigners are killed
The Thirteen Factories become the only legal place for foreign trade with China
The British capture the city during the First Opium War
Communist forces take Guangzhou on 14 October

sections.origins:
Guangzhou stands on the Pearl River, on its eastern bank in the old town near Baiyun Mountain, about 80 miles (130 kilometres) from the river's junction with the South China Sea. The old town commanded the alluvial plain of the Pearl River Delta, with its connection to the sea protected at the Humen Strait. Before the Han conquest the area was inhabited by indigenous, non-Chinese tribes known collectively as the Baiyue. A settlement now known as Nanwucheng was present in the area by 1100 BCE, and some traditional Chinese histories placed its founding in the reign of King Nan of Zhou (314 to 256 BCE). It was said to have been little more than a stockade of bamboo and mud.

The town known as Panyu was founded on the eastern bank of the Pearl River in 214 BCE. The origin of the name Panyu is uncertain; eleven explanations have been offered, including that it referred to two local mountains. The city's nicknames come from the Temple of the Five Immortals, where five stones were said to be the rams ridden by the Taoist culture heroes credited with introducing rice cultivation around the time of the city's foundation.
sections.growth:
Panyu was the seat of the Qin Empire's Nanhai Commandery and served as a base for the first invasion of the Baiyue lands in southern China. Under Nanyue it was a commercial centre: archaeologists have found in it remains from central China, Southeast Asia, India and even Africa. The Old Book of Tang described Guangzhou as an important port in southern China, and direct routes connected the Middle East and China. Medieval Persians such as Al-Masudi and Ibn Khordadbeh knew the city as Khanfu.

Odoric of Pordenone wrote that Guangzhou was as large as three Venices in area and rivalled all of Italy in the amount of crafts it produced. Ibn Battuta visited in the 14th century and described how the Chinese built their large ships in the port's shipyards. After the Qing took Taiwan in 1683 foreign trade revived: the Portuguese, Spaniards, English, French, Dutch, Danish and Swedish companies and later American ships came. By then Guangzhou was one of the world's greatest ports, organised under the Canton System, and its main exports were tea and porcelain. The Thirteen Factories were the only legal place to conduct foreign trade with China from 1757 to 1842.
sections.rulers:
Panyu was the seat of the Qin Empire's Nanhai Commandery. When the Qin fell, General Zhao Tuo established the kingdom of Nanyue and made Panyu its capital in 204 BCE. In 196 BCE he negotiated recognition of his independence in exchange for nominal submission to the Han. After Zhao Mo and Zhao Yingqi, the minister Lü Jia killed the Han ambassadors and the king Zhao Xing in a coup, and Emperor Wu of Han sent six armies that took Panyu and annexed Nanyue by the end of 111 BCE. Panyu then became a provincial capital, and in 226 CE it became the seat of Guang Prefecture, which gave the city its modern name.

After the Tang, the Later Liang governor Liu Yan used Panyu as the base of a Great Yue or Southern Han empire that lasted from 917 to 971, and the city was renamed Xingwang Fu. In 1646 Zhu Yuyue declared himself the Shaowu Emperor there as the last stronghold of the Ming empire. Under the Republic it was the seat of governments led by Sun Yat-sen, and from 1923 to 1926 the base of the Kuomintang. It briefly served as capital of the Republican government in 1949.
sections.life:
The area's population was at first the indigenous Baiyue. The 19th-century city was mostly of one- or two-storey buildings, with a few exceptions such as the Flower Pagoda of the Temple of the Six Banyan Trees and the Five-Story Pagoda. Brick walls about 6 miles (10 kilometres) in circumference, 25 feet high and 20 feet wide enclosed it, with eight main gates and two water gates guarded by day and closed at night. A partition wall divided the northern old town from the southern new town, and the suburb of Xiguan lay beyond. Boats of fishers, traders and Tanka boat people almost entirely concealed about 4 miles of the riverbank. Homes often had a storefront facing the street and used their courtyards as warehouses.

The city held many faiths. The Zhizhi Temple was founded in 233 and has been known as the Guangxiao Temple since the Ming. The Huaisheng Mosque is said to have been built in 627 by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and the city had communities of Persians, Jews, Christians and Parsis in the Tang. Nestorian Christians arrived along the Silk Road but were essentially extinct by the year 1000. The Sacred Heart Cathedral was built from 1861 to 1888. Cantonese is the local language, with Cantonese cuisine, opera and embroidery, and a Hakka population also lived in the surrounding districts.
sections.crises:
Arab and Persian pirates sacked the city on 30 October 758, during the An Lushan Rebellion. In the Guangzhou massacre of 878 the rebel Huang Chao killed about 200,000 Arab, Persian and other foreigners, along with the city's Jews, Christians and Parsis, and the port was closed for fifty years. The Ming imposed sea bans, and the maritime intendancy of Guangzhou was closed in 1384. When the Portuguese arrived in 1516 and the following year, and were accused of piracy and the enslavement of Chinese children, the Guangzhou administration defeated them at the Battle of Tunmen and executed 23 by lingchi.

On 20 January 1647 the Ming turncoat Li Chengdong sacked the city for the Qing and executed Zhu Yuyue. After a prolonged siege, Shang Kexi's forces captured it on 24 November 1650 and killed up to 70,000 Ming loyalists and civilians. The British captured it on 18 March 1841 in the First Opium War. The Punti and Hakka waged clan wars from 1855 to 1867 in which one million people died, and the foreign trade facilities were destroyed in the Arrow War of 1856 to 1858. The Japanese occupied it by the end of December 1938. In 1949 retreating Nationalist forces blew up the Haizhu Bridge, and in the Cultural Revolution many temples, churches and other monuments were destroyed.
sections.legacy:
Guangzhou's trade shaped the modern world economy: as a meeting place of merchants from all over the world it became a major contributor to the rise of the modern global economy. After the 1842 treaty it lost its privileged trade status, and trade moved to Hong Kong and Shanghai, though it remained an entrepôt. In June 1919 the demolition of the city wall began to make way for wider streets and tramways, and it took three years. Its revolutionary history includes the uprisings of 1895 and 1911, honoured in the 72 Martyrs of Huanghuagang Park, and the Whampoa Military Academy, where Sun Yat-sen and Chiang Kai-shek trained an armed force with Soviet help.

Cantonese, Cantonese cuisine and Cantonese opera belong to the whole Guangdong region. Many overseas Chinese have ties to the city, particularly in the United States, Canada and Australia. After 1949 housing was built on the banks of the Pearl River to settle the boat people on land. In 2000 Huadu and Panyu joined the municipality, and the 2020 census counted 18,676,605 people in its administrative area. Guangzhou is today the capital of Guangdong and the centre of the Pearl River Delta.

summary: Guangzhou, founded as Panyu in 214 BCE, was the capital of Nanyue, a port tied to the Middle East and Southeast Asia, and from 1757 to 1842 the only legal site of foreign trade with China. It later became a revolutionary base and is now the capital of Guangdong.
references: John Henry Gray, Walks in the City of Canton (De Souza & Co., 1875)
John E. Wills Jr., China and Maritime Europe, 1500–1800: Trade, Settlement, Diplomacy, and Missions (Cambridge University Press, 2010)
notes: Only the city's own article was available; no 'History of Guangzhou' file. Nothing outside it was used.
START: article says Panyu founded 214 BC; also Nanwucheng by 1100 BC (traditional histories place it under King Nan of Zhou). I used 214 BCE, circa false, with Nanwucheng in the text.

The article gives the sack of 30 Oct 758 and, in the Islam section, says the port was 'subsequently closed for fifty years' after Huang Chao in 878 / also after 758 in the Islam section. The History says the port was closed fifty years after the 878 destruction; the Islam section attaches the closing to 758. I followed the History section only.
The Yangzhou massacre (760) omitted. 'About 200,000' for 878 is as the article gives it.
'By the 1780s' in growth is my paraphrase of 'By that time' after the 1784 and 1788 ships; check. Medieval Persian name Khanfu is from the Toponymy section.

Life: 'Persians, Jews, Christians and Parsis in the Tang' rests on the article's 878 passage and the Islam section (ties since Tang); the Huaisheng Mosque is attributed ('is said to', article says 'renowned for ... built in 627 by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas'). I hedged; the article itself does not hedge, so the editor may check this. Hakka population statement is from Demographics.

Rulers: Guangzhou briefly capital of the Republican government in 1949 (article: 'closing months before total Communist victory'); Sun Yat-sen governments 1917, 1920, 1923. The 1646 Zhu Yuyue declaration is given as 11 December in the article.

Legacy: 'Guangzhou's trade shaped the modern world economy' softened from the article's 'became a major contributor to the rise of the modern global economy'; the line is a close restatement and the editor may reword. Huanghuagang: article says 72 revolutionaries whose bodies were found are honoured there; I wrote 'buried', which the article does not say; editor should change to 'honoured at'.

Left out: the 1927 Guangzhou Uprising, the Canton Coup of 1926, the Shakee Massacre, the Luso-Chinese Accord of 1554, the Red Turban Rebellion, railways, and everything on economy, sport, tourism, airports and metro.
The 1646-47 chronology: Zhu Yuyue 'deposed and executed on January 20, 1647' by Li Chengdong, who 'sacked the city'. Two sentences in crises/rulers follow that.
The ancient article text on Panyu's founding includes garbled sentences about Tang records of trade missions and 'records on foreign trade ships reach upon til the late 20th century'; left out.
